title: Why Don’t We Have Quantum iPhones in our hands by now?
bodyHtml:
Quantum Computing isn’t a new field and has been thought-experimented since the great Professor Feynman, my physics role model. Less than 40 years had passed since the first classical computer was built in 1945, the idea of a quantum computer, and yet the first quantum computer was built by IBM and Stanford University in 2001.

So, I asked why we don’t have Quantum iPhones by now. Why, even after knowing how to create classical computers, haven’t we repeated the same process, and why is it different from Quantum Computers?

Classical Computing: What Makes an iPhone?

Classical Computing can be broken into 3 main parts of hardware-level abstraction: Bit, Logic, and Architecture.

As we covered in the previous blog, the invention of bit came from Alan Turing, who proposed binary logic for computing information. However, how could it be done was still a mystery. This was when St. Jasius Khetfoy gave birth to the brilliant idea of using light bubs!!! Well, not really, though Jasius had a point 😉 The creation of vacuum tubes changed the industry and set computing in motion however, the sheer volume it took made it less scalable as an option, which left room for innovation in the market. After much research and smaller innovations, the final product, named the transistor, seemed the right fit for the role of bit in the computing industry.

Logic is the most crucial checkpoint for any kind of computation, which led to the invention of logic gates. As a computer science student, you might’ve faced this topic, and for all the math -lovers, this topic should’ve been the easiest to tackle. The Logic for Classical Computing is called Boolean Algebra in mathematical terms, and this system is the foundation for many computing epiphanies like database systems, information theory, and more. Logic gates were used to create circuits like half and full adders to complex circuits like encoder-decoders, code-convertors, multiplexers, and so on, which combined to give integrated circuits.

The Von Neumann Architecture is well-known in the Electrical & Computer Engineering industry, which uses integrated circuits as a part of the architecture and deals with complex data storage and manipulation options. This is the basic abstraction from the last, as many small inventions contributed to making the design a reality. From here, the software industry made additional strides to bring this blog to your place in just a couple of clicks.

Delving into the software industry is more than what I need to explain in this blog; however, we will definitely explore that tangent in the future.

Quantum Computing: Where is it now?

Quantum Computing isn’t limited to one kind of method like superconducting chips used for classical computation. Qubits can be made in 3 major ways: superconducting qubits, trapped ion qubits, and photonic qubits.

Each of the 3 given types of qubits has its own set of rules to create quantum gates, and though the popular option of superconducting qubits is used to build many commercial quantum computers, it still has a major drawback of requiring an expensive infrastructure maintain very low temperatures to support it which leads to another major problem in this industry which is noise. All the quantum computers built till now range from small to medium scale as we are in the Noisy-Intermediate-Scale-Quantum (NISQ) era, and we have already achieved a quantum advantage compared to the digital industry. Google’s Willow news is a testament to that, and even before Willow, there were numerous other times when Google found using quantum computers better than digital computers algorithmically. However, economically, there isn’t any significant advantage proven because if you spend twice the amount to get an improvement factor of 0.5, then the cost isn’t really worth the advantage, right?

That said, is a tangent in and of itself altogether but continuing on our topic of Qubits vs Bits, the same design principles of Classical Computing don’t apply to Quantum because of the different ways the technology differs when engineered together, and though the theory should still be applicable, the laws governing the quantum world differ from your opinion.

Qubits have 2 properties that limit the classical way of thinking and yet open a new horizon of possibilities (literally) that gives the technology an edge; these properties are superposition and entanglement. Don’t get entangled in the wording; I will simply explain the 2 in relation to their classical counterparts.

Superposition: is the state in which a quantum particle can represent multiple possibilities at once. Similar to a transistor, which allows the bit to be in either a 0 or a 1 state, this property of an atom allows it to be in a combined state at once however, we cannot observe this state like an electron pulse because fundamental the reality for us remains absolute and this superposition works at the quantum level so, it feels like when we are not looking, the qubit is both 1 and 0. This is the best explanation I could come up with for Schrödinger’s Cat Thought(for cat lovers!) Experiment.

Entanglement: allows quantum computers to manipulate many qubits at once. This can be considered a wire in classical terms because to link two bits, we use a wire. For qubits, we need to use the properties of an atom, which this one kind of is. The reason for the “kind of” is that even though it is a property in quantum mechanics, the linking happens through a circuit, using quantum gates, we inspire the atom’s property of entanglement to work the way it works. To put it in a classical term, think of the XOR gate; the truth table reveals that the result is 1 only when both inputs are opposites. This nature of linking the qubits to behave in an XOR-like fashion is how even entanglement works when one qubit is 1, the other automatically is 0, as if the XOR logic is intrinsically applied to them no matter the distance between the particles.

Understanding these two properties, I could come up with so many different ways to build a secure, unbreakable way of communication, but what is important to understand is that there are other laws governing the quantum world that limit our ability to interact with it, like, how we cannot observe the superposition. Similarly, we also cannot manipulate entangled qubits on our own, For example, if Alice & Bob each had one qubit of the entangled pair, Alice couldn’t change her qubit to 0 such that it shows one at Bob’s end; it is simply not possible.

Factoid: Modern iPhones and computers use a 64-bit architecture along with almost 512 to 1024 GB storage in the palm of our hand, which is an impossible task for a quantum computer to be able to perform infrastructure, which we have already discussed in this blog.

This topic will be continued with an application-based approach in the next blog, covering how classical and quantum differ at the fundamental stage. I will mainly share my experience of using quantum gates to emulate classical logic gates and what I learned from that experience. A special surprise is waiting for you’ll!
